legacy_conversion_note: Original source (source/Y3/Session 2/Medical Statician/Case Study_ Medical Statistician.docx -- no separate Guide Notes document exists for this case, confirmed by checking the folder) is a real-shaped pharmaceutical-statistics scenario -- the protagonist Tanya Teeples (8 years at Bansky Pharmaceuticals, 3 years freelance, MS Healthcare Statistics from USC), her boss James Miller, the fictional drug Paxovir (weekly-injection canine diabetes treatment), the $600,000 total budget with its $23,000 design and $84,000 analysis line items, the $15/dose/week x 26-week treatment cost, the 1-month launch / 7-month conclusion window, the canine-diabetes prevalence/risk-factor claims (1 in 300, ages 4-14, unspayed females 2x, the named at-risk breeds), and the four probability / four non-probability sampling method names are all preserved verbatim or near-verbatim from the source. The source's own dilemma was open-ended ('probability sampling OR non-probability sampling,' each an umbrella of 4 unnamed sub-methods) rather than SPEC-compliant binary -- resolved per the human-approved lock in cases/_concepts/LEGACY_DILEMMA_LOCKS_2026-08-20.md ('medical-statician' entry), which names one concrete method per side: simple random sampling from the general population (A) vs. convenience sampling through partner clinics (B). The source's own canine-diabetes prevalence/breed/risk claims (originally attributed to 'Braxtons.com,' an unverifiable blog source) were re-verified against a real veterinary pharmaceutical source (Merck Animal Health's Vetsulin diabetes page, S1) during this conversion -- the figures matched almost exactly (same 1-in-300 prevalence, same 4-14 age range, same 2x unspayed-female risk), with two breeds (Golden Retriever, Labrador Retriever) from the original's 12-breed list dropped because the re-verification source's fetched content only confirmed 10 of the 12 breed names; the case now cites only the 10 independently re-confirmed breeds rather than repeating the unverified pair. The source's own referenced margin-of-error calculator (SurveyMonkey) is preserved and its underlying formula (z=1.96 at 95% confidence) reproduced in-document per case-research's link-survives-death rule. The source gave no real, publicly sourceable per-dog recruitment cost for either sampling method (an unavoidable NOT FOUND -- no veterinary-specific recruitment-cost benchmark exists in the public literature); per SPEC.md section 5's three exits, this conversion takes the Stated Modeling Assumption exit (MA1/MA2, Appendix G), building the assumed values from real, cited human multi-site clinical-trial per-patient recruitment-cost literature (S5: mean $277/patient, range $74-$797 across sites in the same real study) rather than an unfounded guess, and disclosing the values openly rather than burying them in a sourced-looking table. New appendices not in the original source were added during this conversion to support the primary metric and the regulatory-rigor argument: Appendix D (recruitment cost benchmarks), Appendix E (margin-of-error formula reproduced in-document), and Appendix F (the real FDA CVM regulatory standard for new animal drug study design, 21 CFR 514.117 and GFI #266, grounding Option A's real regulatory-rigor advantage in an actual federal citation rather than an assertion). The balance test is satisfied on the case's chosen primary metric (margin of error at the maximum affordable sample size): Option B's lower per-subject recruitment cost buys a larger affordable sample and a lower (better) margin of error, beating Option A by 15.5% -- comfortably under SPEC section 2's 20% cap -- while Option A retains a real, separately disclosed regulatory-rigor advantage (randomization minimizing bias, the actual legal standard cited in Appendix F) that the dollar-based primary metric does not capture, which is what keeps both options genuinely defensible rather than the case being a disguised landslide on cost alone.

deliverables.text: A stated total sample size (number of dogs) for your chosen sampling method, with the arithmetic shown step by step.
A sampling-method comparison table naming the specific probability or non-probability method chosen and why the other three in its category were rejected.
A specific plan for how you would actually draw your sample from the population -- which regions, clinics, or owner records, and why.
A total estimated cost and time for your chosen sampling method, shown against the $600,000 budget and 7-month deadline, with dollars-remaining stated.
The margin of error expected at a 95% confidence level for your study's sample size, with the calculation shown.
At least two original visual displays comparing your chosen method against the alternative on sample size, cost, and margin of error.

balance.argument_a: Option A (simple random sampling from the general U.S. dog population) is the only method that produces a randomized study meeting the exact legal standard FDA regulation sets for 'adequate and well-controlled' -- assignment/selection that 'is random and minimizes bias' (21 CFR 514.117, Appendix F). It generalizes to the whole population Bansky ultimately wants to sell Paxovir to, not just the breed/clinic mix its own partner network happens to already treat.
balance.argument_b: Option B (convenience sampling through partner clinics) buys a dramatically lower cost per enrolled subject ($90 vs. $250 in the case's disclosed recruitment-cost assumption, Appendix G) within the shared $493,000 budget, which affords a larger sample (1,027 vs. 770 dogs) and therefore a lower, better margin of error (about 3.06% vs. 3.53% at 95% confidence) on the case's primary graded metric -- a real, computed 15.5% advantage, comfortably inside SPEC's 20% balance cap.
balance.margin_basis: Max affordable N = $493,000 / (recruitment cost/subject + $390 drug cost/subject) for each option, using Appendix G's MA1/MA2 recruitment-cost assumptions; margin of error computed at that N via Appendix E's formula (z=1.96, p=0.5); margin_pct = percent difference between the two options' margin-of-error results.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Recruitment cost per subject, Option A
modeling_assumptions.basis: Below the real $277 mean per-patient recruitment cost across sites in a cited multi-site human study (S5). This figure is taken as an ALL-IN per-enrolled-subject cost -- i.e. it already stands in for whatever screening/outreach effort it takes to locate and enroll one subject, the same way the $277 human-trial benchmark implicitly includes each site's own patient-finding effort, not just a flat administrative fee. It is NOT stacked on top of Appendix B's 1-in-300 diabetic-dog prevalence figure as an additional per-contact multiplier -- Appendix B's 300:1 ratio explains WHY Option A's real-world recruitment is harder and slower than B's (motivating a higher per-subject figure than MA2's $90), but it is not a second cost layer to multiply through the $250 estimate. A Hero who tries to apply Appendix B's 300x ratio as a literal multiplier on top of MA1's $250 will blow the $493,000 budget by roughly two orders of magnitude -- see FACILITATOR.md's second trap.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The answer is sensitive to this value.

modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The answer is sensitive to this value.

sensitivity_note: The margin between Options A and B is driven by MA1/MA2 (the disclosed recruitment-cost-per-subject assumptions). See sensitivity_model.py and FACILITATOR.md for the +/-50% flex analysis.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: No public, veterinary-specific per-subject recruitment-cost figure exists (RESEARCH_LOG.md P05, a genuine NOT FOUND). MA1's $250/subject is a documented good-faith estimate built from the closest real public analogue -- peer-reviewed human multi-site clinical-trial recruitment-cost literature (source S5: mean $277/patient, range $74-$797 across sites in the same real study) -- not an invented figure, but not a direct citation for the actual veterinary quantity either. A +50% flex breaks SPEC section 2's 20% balance cap (margin rises to 26.3%), which is why this is disclosed here rather than silently left unstable.

Same NOT FOUND and same real-analogue basis as recruit_cost_a_usd (RESEARCH_LOG.md P05, source S5). MA2's $90/subject sits near the cited range's low/efficient end (the $72-online, $74-cheapest-site figures), a documented good-faith estimate, not an invented figure. A -50% flex breaks the 20% cap (margin rises to 21.3%), which is why this is disclosed here rather than silently left unstable.
